Read the Move action instead

Your keyboard code works, but it lists every key by hand, so you now swap it for the project’s own Move input action, which gives you the same direction in one line and keeps working when you add other controls.

An input action is a named input, such as Move or Jump, that the project’s Input System asset connects to real keys. Your project already has one. The InputSystem_Actions asset in the Assets folder has a Player map with Move, Look, Attack, Interact, Crouch, Jump, Previous, Next and Sprint. Move gives you a Vector2, which is one value holding two numbers: x for left and right, y for forward and back. The W, A, S and D keys are already connected to it, and diagonals are already length 1.

page.text: `private InputAction moveAction;` is a variable that holds one input action. `InputSystem.actions.FindAction("Move")` looks the action up by its name, once, in `Start`. The name in quotes must match exactly, capital M included. `moveAction.ReadValue<Vector2>()` asks for its current value as a Vector2, so you get (0, 0) when nothing is held and a direction when keys are down. In `FixedUpdate`, `new Vector3(moveInput.x, 0f, moveInput.y)` puts the action’s y into the z slot, because the ball moves along the floor. The rest is the same push as before.

page.title: Why switch?
page.text: The keyboard version taught you how a key becomes a number. The action version is shorter, and the connection between keys and Move lives in the project’s Input System asset instead of in your code. Later in the course, a jump or a menu key is one more `FindAction` away.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Likely causes if the ball does not move or the Console shows an error:

NullReferenceException: Object reference not set to an instance of an object, pointing at the `ReadValue` line. `FindAction` found nothing, so check that the name in quotes is exactly Move.

error CS0246: The type or namespace name ‘InputAction’ could not be found. The line `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;` is missing at the top of the file.

The ball does not move and there is no error. Click once inside the Game view first, then check that Speed is not 0 in the Inspector.

Make the camera follow the ball

page.caption: CameraFollow.cs

page.text: `public Transform target;` is a variable that holds the position, rotation and scale of another object. Because it is public, it shows in the Inspector as **Target**, and you fill it by dragging Player onto it. `transform` with a small t is the Transform of the object this script is on, which is the camera. An offset is the gap between two positions. `transform.position - target.position` subtracts one Vector3 from another, which gives the gap, and you keep it in `offset`. `LateUpdate` adds that gap to the target’s position every frame, so the camera sits the same distance away wherever the ball goes. The camera never turns, so the ball can roll without the view spinning.

page.title: Why a script, and why LateUpdate
page.text: You could make the camera a child of the ball, but then it would roll and spin with it. A script that copies only the position keeps the view steady. `LateUpdate` runs after the frame’s `Update` methods. This lets the camera follow a target after movement performed in `Update`. The ball moves on the physics clock; its Rigidbody’s **Interpolate** setting smooths its displayed position between physics steps.

The camera does not move and there is no error. CameraFollow is on the wrong object. Click Main Camera and look for the Camera Follow (Script) section.

You should see a ball that rolls in every direction, coasts to a stop, and stays near the middle of the view, with no red messages in the Console. It went wrong if a red message appears or the camera lags or jumps: go back to the Stuck? list in the part that covers it.
Challenges
These challenges have no steps, because working out how to change code is how it sticks. Save your work first, keep Play off while you edit, and read the Console if something breaks.

Challenge: add a jump. Change PlayerController so pressing Space gives the ball one upward push each time you press it. The push shows in the Inspector as **Jump Force** with a starting value of 5. Rolling still works. For now the ball may jump again while it is already in the air, and that is fine. Test it in your head: with Jump Force 5 and a Mass of 1, one press launches the ball upward at about 5 units per second, so it rises roughly one unit and falls back. Holding Space down does not keep launching it, because only the frame of the press counts.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Space is a key, so you can read it with `Keyboard.current.spaceKey.wasPressedThisFrame`, which is true only on the frame the key goes down. A frame can pass between two physics steps, so a press could be missed if you tested it in FixedUpdate. Declare `private bool jumpRequested;` alongside your other variables. In `Update`, set it to true only when a press occurs: `if (Keyboard.current != null && Keyboard.current.spaceKey.wasPressedThisFrame) { jumpRequested = true; }`. Leave it unchanged on frames without a press, so the request survives until `FixedUpdate` consumes it. Then, in FixedUpdate, jump if the bool is true and set it back to false. Use `rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse);`. An impulse is a push all at once, so it suits a single jump. Check `Keyboard.current` is not null first.

Optional challenge: cap the top speed. Add a **Max Speed** field with a starting value of 8. Whatever the keys do, the ball’s flat speed, along x and z, never goes above Max Speed, while falling and jumping are not slowed. Test it in your head: set Max Speed to 4 and hold W. The ball speeds up, reaches 4 and stays there. Let go, and it still coasts to a stop. If you did the jump challenge, jumping still works.

page.title: Hint
page.text:
`rb.linearVelocity` is the ball’s velocity vector. Its flat speed is the length of its x and z parts. For this challenge, replace the horizontal `rb.AddForce(direction * speed);` line with the following lines, keeping each inside `FixedUpdate`:

`Vector3 flat = new Vector3(rb.linearVelocity.x, 0f, rb.linearVelocity.z);`

`Vector3 requested = flat + direction * (speed / rb.mass) * Time.fixedDeltaTime;`

`Vector3 limited = Vector3.ClampMagnitude(requested, maxSpeed);`

`rb.AddForce(limited - flat, ForceMode.VelocityChange);`

The requested velocity includes the change that your original force would produce during the upcoming physics step. `Vector3.ClampMagnitude` limits its length while leaving smaller values unchanged. `ForceMode.VelocityChange` applies the resulting change directly, so this calculation uses `Time.fixedDeltaTime` explicitly. The change has no y component, so jumping and falling still work. Remove the original horizontal force call; leaving it in would add another push after your limit calculation. To check the simulated flat speed, temporarily log it in `Update` with `Debug.Log(new Vector3(rb.linearVelocity.x, 0f, rb.linearVelocity.z).magnitude);`, then remove that line.

For the jump, Space gives one push per press and rolling still works. For the cap, the ball never rolls faster than Max Speed. It went wrong if the jump fires repeatedly while Space is held (you are using isPressed, not wasPressedThisFrame) or if the ball floats when falling (you set the y part of the velocity to 0 in the cap).
Wrap-up

You can now read the keyboard with Keyboard.current or the Move action, push a Rigidbody from FixedUpdate, and write a script that keeps the camera behind the ball. Test yourself. How do you read whether A is held in this project, and why not Input.GetKey? Why is AddForce called in FixedUpdate and not in Update? What does the camera script store in Start, and why does it move in LateUpdate? Next week the arena fills with spinning pickups. You will collect them using triggers and tags, show a score and a win message in TextMeshPro, and finish Orb Collector.

l_9e49f2c4974f.summary: Collect spinning pickups using triggers and tags, show a score and win message in TextMeshPro; submit Orb Collector as a recording and screenshot.
keyIdeas: A trigger is a collider with Is Trigger ticked. Things pass through it, and Unity still calls OnTriggerEnter in your script. At least one of the two objects needs a Rigidbody, and your Player ball already has one.
A tag is a label on an object. Inside OnTriggerEnter, other.CompareTag(“Pickup”) asks whether the thing you touched carries that label, so only pickups count.
A counter is a whole number that starts at 0 and grows by one each time something happens. An if statement runs its block only when a condition is true, such as the counter reaching the target.
Text on screen is a TMP_Text on a Canvas. Your script sets its text property, and you connect it by dragging the object into a field in the Inspector.

vocabulary.definition: A collider with Is Trigger ticked, which lets other objects pass through it while still telling your code that they entered.
A method Unity calls for you, once, when your object’s collider enters a trigger.
A label you put on an object so that code can tell what kind of object it is.
A method that asks whether an object carries a given tag, such as other.CompareTag(“Pickup”).
A line of code that runs its block only when a condition is true.
A whole number, such as score, that starts at 0 and goes up by one each time something happens.
A method that removes an object from the scene.
The type that holds TextMeshPro text, whose text property your script sets to change what the screen shows.
The flat layer that holds on-screen text and buttons so they stay in front of the game.

study.overview: This week you finished Orb Collector. The ball now collects spinning pickups, the game counts them, and the screen shows a score and a win message. You can now make a trigger, detect it in code, pick out the right objects with a tag, count with an if statement, and put text on screen with TextMeshPro. Reread this page before next week, because Dodge builds on the same ideas.

points.heading: Detect a touch with a trigger and OnTriggerEnter
points.explanation: A trigger is a collider with Is Trigger ticked. Other objects pass through it, but Unity still calls `OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)` in your script. At least one of the two objects needs a Rigidbody, and your Player ball already has one. The method name must be spelled exactly, with a capital T and E, or Unity never calls it and gives no warning. Inside it, `other` is the collider you touched. Example: you ticked Is Trigger on the Box Collider of Pickup and put PickupCollector on Player. When the ball rolled into the pickup, the ball passed through it and the Console printed Picked up Pickup. To remove the object, use `Destroy(other.gameObject)`, not `Destroy(other)`, because `other` is only the collider and you want to remove the whole object.

points.heading: Tell pickups apart with a tag, and count with an if statement
points.explanation: A tag is a label on an object. `other.CompareTag("Pickup")` asks whether the thing you touched carries that label, so only pickups count and everything else is ignored. The word in the code and the tag in the Inspector must match exactly, including the capital P. A counter is a whole number that starts at 0: `private int score = 0;`. Each time the if block runs, `score = score + 1;` takes the old value, adds one, and stores it back. A second if, `if (score >= totalPickups)`, runs its block only when the condition is true. Example: with eight tagged pickups and Total Pickups set to 8, the score goes from 0 up to 8, and the win check becomes true only on the eighth pickup. If You win! appears too early, check that Total Pickups reads 8 and count the pickups in the Hierarchy.

points.heading: Show the score and a win message with TMP_Text
points.explanation: On-screen text is a TMP_Text on a Canvas. Add `using TMPro;` at the top of the script, then declare `[SerializeField] private TMP_Text scoreText;`. The field appears in the Inspector, and you connect it by dragging ScoreText from the Hierarchy onto the Score Text field on Player. Your script then sets the words with `scoreText.text = "Score: " + score + " / " + totalPickups;`. Put that line in your own method, `UpdateScoreText`, and call it from Start and after each pickup, so the screen always matches the counter. The win message works the same way: WinText is emptied in Start with `winText.text = "";` and set to `"You win!"` only when the if finds that the score has reached the total. Example: at Score: 2 / 8, six pickups are left and the win text is empty. If you see a NullReferenceException, a field in the Inspector is empty, so drag the text object onto it.

page.text: Last week your ball learned to roll and the camera learned to follow. This week the arena fills with spinning pickups, and the ball gets a job. You will make the pickups spin, detect the ball with a trigger, tell pickups apart with a tag, count them with an if statement, and show a score and a win message in TextMeshPro. By Sunday you will have a finished Orb Collector that you can play from the first pickup to the win message.

page.text: Line by line. `[SerializeField] private float degreesPerSecond = 90f;` makes a number you can change in the Inspector. It starts at 90, so one full turn takes four seconds. `Update` runs once per frame, so the pickup turns a little each frame. `transform.Rotate` turns the object by the three angles you give it, one for each of the X, Y and Z axes. Only the middle one, Y, is not zero. `Time.deltaTime` is the number of seconds the last frame took. Multiplying by it means the pickup turns at the same speed on a fast computer and a slow one. `Space.World` makes the turn happen around the world’s vertical line, so your tilted cube spins like a top instead of tumbling.

page.transcript:
Hello. Last week your ball learned to move. This week it gets a job: collecting things. Let me explain three ideas, then you will build them.

First, collisions and triggers. A collider is the shape that physics uses to feel the world. Normally two colliders meet and push each other. Your ball hits the arena wall and stops. A trigger is a collider with Is Trigger ticked. It does not push anything. Other objects pass straight through it, but Unity still tells your code that something went in. That is exactly what a pickup needs. The ball rolls through, and your code decides what happens.

The message arrives as a method called OnTriggerEnter. Unity calls it for you, once, when another collider enters the trigger. It hands you a Collider called other, which is whatever came in. One rule: at least one of the two objects needs a Rigidbody. Your ball already has one.

Second, tags. The ball cannot yet tell a pickup from anything else it might touch later, like a hazard. A tag is a label you stick on an object. Your code then asks other.CompareTag, with the label in quotation marks. The spelling and the capital letters must match exactly.

Third, the if statement. It says: only run this block when a condition is true. If the thing I touched is tagged Pickup, then destroy it and add one to the score. The score is a counter, a whole number that starts at zero and goes up by one each time. A second if checks whether the counter has reached the target, and if so shows the win message.

To show text on screen you will use TextMeshPro. Your script keeps a TMP_Text, sets its text property, and the screen updates.

Build it one small step at a time, and test after each step.

page.text: `void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)` is a method with a name Unity already knows. Unity calls it for you whenever the object this script is on moves into a trigger. The spelling and capitals must be exact, or Unity never calls it and nothing tells you why. `other` is a box that holds the collider of whatever you touched. `Debug.Log` prints a message in the Console, and `other.name` is the name of the object you touched. `Destroy(other.gameObject)` removes that whole object from the scene. It is `other.gameObject`, not `other`, because `other` is only the collider, and you want to remove the object that owns it.

You put the script on Player so one counter tracks every pickup the ball collects. Unity can send trigger messages to scripts on both objects involved. Player already has the Rigidbody needed for these trigger interactions.

Tag the pickups and keep score with an if statement
Right now the ball would destroy anything it touched that is a trigger. A tag lets the code collect only pickups, and a counter lets it count them.

page.text: `private int score = 0;` is the counter. `int` means a whole number, and it starts at 0. `if (other.CompareTag("Pickup"))` runs the block in curly braces only when the object you touched carries the Pickup tag. Anything else is ignored. `score = score + 1;` reads as: take the old score, add one, and store the result back in score. `score >= totalPickups` is true when the score is 8 or more, so the second `if` runs only when the last pickup is collected. `>=` means greater than or equal to. The `+` between text and numbers in `Debug.Log` joins them into one message.

The pickups you copy keep the tag, the trigger and the spin script, so you only set where each one goes. If your arena is smaller than that, keep every pickup inside its walls by choosing smaller numbers in the same pattern.

Show the score on screen with TextMeshPro

Players do not read the Console. They read the screen, so you now put the score where the player can see it. Text on screen uses TextMeshPro, and a Canvas is the flat layer that holds all on-screen text and buttons.

page.text: `using TMPro;` lets your script use TextMeshPro types. `TMP_Text` is the type that holds any TextMeshPro text, and marking the field `[SerializeField]` makes it appear in the Inspector so you can drag ScoreText into it. `UpdateScoreText` is a method you wrote yourself. It builds the words and sets `scoreText.text`, and the screen shows the new words. `Start` runs once when the game begins, so the text shows Score: 0 / 8 straight away. Calling `UpdateScoreText();` is how you run your own method.

page.text: Use the checkpoint file only if your own project does not work and you cannot find why. Unzip it (Extract All on Windows, double-click on a Mac) and open the unzipped folder from the Projects screen in Unity Hub. When this part checks out, you are ready for your Weekly builds item.

You should see Score: 0 / 8 at the start, a score that rises with every pickup, and You win! only after the eighth. Gone wrong looks like this: You win! shows from the start (WinText was not emptied, so the script is out of date or Win Text is empty), or it never shows (fewer than eight pickups have the Pickup tag, or Total Pickups is not 8).

1. NullReferenceException when Start sets the win message. Stop Play, select Player, and check the Win Text field in Pickup Collector (Script). If it is empty, drag WinText onto it. 2. You win! appears too early. Click Player and check that Total Pickups reads 8, and count the pickups in the Hierarchy. 3. The ball cannot reach a pickup. It sits outside or inside a wall. Select it and move its Position inside the arena.
Challenges
These challenges have no steps, because working out how to change code is how it sticks. Save your work first, keep Play off while you edit, and read the Console if something breaks.

Challenge: count down. Change the score text so it shows how many pickups are left instead of how many you have. At the start it reads Left: 8. After you collect three it reads Left: 5. The You win! message still appears when the number reaches 0. Test it in your head: with Total Pickups 8 and a score of 3, the text must read Left: 5, and with a score of 8 it must read Left: 0 and show the win message.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Only `UpdateScoreText` needs to change. The number to show is `totalPickups - score`, which is the total minus what you have already collected. You can build the whole message in one line, the same way the current line joins words and numbers with `+`.

Optional challenge: a hazard. Make a red cube named Hazard in the arena and give it a new tag, Hazard, with Is Trigger ticked. When the ball touches it, the ball returns to its starting position and stops moving. With Play off, select Player and note its starting Position. Use those X, Y and Z values in the hint’s Vector3 instead of 0, 0.5, 0 if yours differ. The score stays the same and the hazard stays where it is. Test it in your head: with a score of 3, the ball touches the Hazard, jumps back to the middle, and the text still reads Left: 5. Pickups already collected stay gone.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Add an `else if (other.CompareTag("Hazard"))` block after the Pickup block in OnTriggerEnter. Inside it, set the position with `transform.position = new Vector3(0f, 0.5f, 0f);` and stop its travel with `GetComponent<Rigidbody>().linearVelocity = Vector3.zero;`. On the next line, stop its spin with `GetComponent<Rigidbody>().angularVelocity = Vector3.zero;`. Angular velocity describes how fast the Rigidbody rotates. Release the movement keys while testing the reset, because held keys will push the ball again. Remember that the tag must exist before you can set it.
Wrap-up

You can now make a trigger with Is Trigger and detect it with OnTriggerEnter, pick out pickups with CompareTag, count them with an if statement, and show a score and a win message with TMP_Text. Test yourself. Inside OnTriggerEnter, how do you check that the thing you touched is a pickup? What does the if statement do with the counter, and when does it let the win message appear? Which type holds the text on screen, and how does your script reach it? Next time you start Dodge: a hazard that spawns at random positions on a timer that gets faster and faster, and that you destroy when it is no longer needed.

facilitation.announcement: Welcome to the week where Orb Collector gets finished. This week you make spinning pickups, detect the ball with a trigger, tell pickups apart with a tag, count them with an if statement, and show a score and a win message in TextMeshPro. The one thing to get right: the tag in the Inspector and the word in your code must match exactly, Pickup with a capital P, and ScoreText and WinText must be dragged into their fields on Player. Your first forum post is due Thursday. Replies, the self-check quiz and your Weekly builds submission are due Sunday night. If you are stuck, read the Stuck? list first, then post in the forum with your Console message copied in.
watchFor: Students whose pickups disappear but the score never changes. The tag is still Untagged, or the copies were made before tagging. Ask them to post a screenshot of the Tag row and point them to the stuck list.

Students who put PickupCollector on the Pickup instead of the Player, or who forget Is Trigger. The Console stays empty. Ask which object the script is on and whether the ball goes through the pickup.
UnassignedReferenceException for scoreText or winText. Tell them to drag the Canvas objects into the Player’s fields, and to check the script is saved and compiled.

Students on the old Input class or old code copied from the web, such as FindObjectOfType or rb.velocity. Remind them this course uses the Input System and linearVelocity, and send them back to the page’s code.
Submissions where the recording stops before the win message, or shows a Console with red messages. Ask for a recording that goes through all eight pickups.
feedback: Your trigger works well: the ball passes through and the pickup vanishes at the right moment. Next, try changing totalPickups in the Inspector and watch what the text does.
Your score counts correctly, and I can see the if statement does the checking. Say in your own words in the forum what the line `score >= totalPickups` asks.
The win message appears only after the last pickup, which is what you wanted. Check the Console is free of red messages before you record.
I can see the score on screen but not in your recording from the start. Record from pressing Play so the first Score: 0 / 8 is visible.

(0.6, 0.8, 0), with the action’s y kept as y.
(0, 0.6, 0.8), with the action’s x mapped to y.
(0.8, 0, 0.6), with the action’s x and y swapped.

t_a24fc06ba9a0.explanation: The code puts `moveInput.x` in the Vector3’s x slot, sets its y to zero so the direction stays flat, and puts `moveInput.y` in the z slot. The other options place a value in the vertical y slot or swap the action’s coordinates. Review “Read the Move action instead.”

t_f2b659e6661b.prompt: In one or two sentences, describe what the camera script stores in `Start` and what it does with that value in `LateUpdate`.
t_f2b659e6661b.answer: It stores the offset between the camera and its target in `Start`. In `LateUpdate`, it sets the camera’s position to the target’s current position plus that offset.
t_f2b659e6661b.explanation: The saved offset keeps the camera the same distance from the target as the target moves. `LateUpdate` updates the camera position after the frame’s `Update` methods. Review “Make the camera follow the ball.”

t_fa262e5750e5.prompt:
This week your Orb Collector came alive: pickups spin, the ball triggers them, a tag picks out the right objects, an if statement and a counter keep the score, and TextMeshPro shows it all on screen. Now tell us about your build.

By Sunday night, reply to two classmates. Try their game if they share it, or read their post closely. In each reply, say one thing that works well and one thing you would change, and say why. If a classmate is stuck, suggest something they could check, using what you learned this week.

How posts are graded, every week: full marks for a first post by Thursday that is about your own work and answers the prompt, and two replies by Sunday that each help a classmate go further (say what worked for you, suggest one change, or ask a real question). Late or one-line posts earn half.

t_8eeb75fccbc2.title: Weekly builds: Orb Collector triggers and scoring
t_8eeb75fccbc2.prompt:
Last time, your ball learned to roll. Now you will make it collect tagged pickups, track its score, and show a win message. This build contributes to Weekly builds, which counts for 40% of your course grade.

Customize Orb Collector by choosing a pickup color and arranging the eight pickups in your own pattern inside the arena. Keep the Pickup tags and triggers working, and make sure the score reaches 8 / 8 before You win! appears. Save the scene, then upload to the LMS a short screen recording of a complete playthrough and a screenshot showing the final score and win message. Use MP4 or MOV for the recording and PNG or JPG for the screenshot. Add a brief note explaining your color and layout choices, and note any help you used, including AI tools.

Your work is graded complete or incomplete. The rubric shows how the trigger, score and win message should work, and how to show your own design choices in the submitted evidence.
steps: With Play mode off, choose a color for PickupMaterial and arrange all eight pickups in a pattern of your own inside the arena. Keep the pickups within reach of the ball.
Check that every pickup has the Pickup tag and Box Collider with Is Trigger ticked. Check that Player has PickupCollector, and that Score Text and Win Text are connected in the Inspector.
Play from the start, collect all eight pickups, and confirm the score reaches 8 / 8 before You win! appears. Stop Play mode and save the scene.

Upload a short screen recording of the complete playthrough and a screenshot showing 8 / 8 and You win! to the LMS. Include a brief note explaining your color and layout choices and any help you used.

t_f8e42fe58ab8.prompt: You want the ball to pass through a pickup while Unity detects contact. Which setup works?

choices.text: Remove the pickup collider; keep the Rigidbody on the Player
Tick Is Trigger on the pickup collider; keep the Rigidbody on the Player
Tick Is Kinematic on the Player; leave Is Trigger off
Add a Rigidbody to the pickup; remove the Player’s collider

t_f8e42fe58ab8.explanation: A trigger is a collider with Is Trigger ticked. At least one of the two objects needs a Rigidbody, and the Player already has one. Removing a collider prevents this contact from being detected. Is Kinematic does not make a collider a trigger. Adding a Rigidbody to the pickup is unnecessary, and removing the Player’s collider would prevent contact. Review “Make the pickup a trigger and detect the ball.”

t_4d07adab5387.prompt: The Player touches an object tagged Hazard. Your OnTriggerEnter method only has an if block for other.CompareTag(“Pickup”), and the score increase and Destroy call are inside that block. What happens?

choices.text: The object is destroyed; the score increases by one
The object is destroyed; the score stays the same
The object is ignored; the Pickup block does not run
The score increases by one; the object stays

t_4d07adab5387.explanation: CompareTag(“Pickup”) is false for an object tagged Hazard, so the statements inside that if block do not run. The object is not destroyed and the score does not change. Review “Tag the pickups and keep score with an if statement.”

t_4599979f8420.prompt: You declare a field for the on-screen score in PickupCollector. Which setup lets the script update the TextMeshPro object named ScoreText?

choices.text: Use a TMP_Text field and drag ScoreText into its Inspector field
Use a Rigidbody field and drag ScoreText into its Inspector field
Use a TMP_Text field and type ScoreText as the field’s starting value
Use a GameObject field and rename the script file to ScoreText

t_4599979f8420.explanation: TMP_Text is the TextMeshPro text type. The serialized field appears in the Inspector, where you connect it by dragging ScoreText from the Hierarchy. A Rigidbody field has the wrong type. Typing the object’s name does not assign a reference. Renaming the script does not connect the text object. Review “Show the score on screen with TextMeshPro.”

t_4ba0764eef12.prompt: A valid Pickup trigger enters the Player once. The score is 2 and totalPickups is 6. What is the score after the code runs, and does the condition score >= totalPickups run its block?
t_4ba0764eef12.answer: The score becomes 3. The condition is false, so its block does not run.
t_4ba0764eef12.explanation: The pickup block adds one to the counter, changing 2 to 3. Since 3 is less than 6, score >= totalPickups is false. Review “Count with an if statement.”

t_5399602beb88.prompt: When the Player enters a trigger, Unity can call OnTriggerEnter on a script attached to the Player.

choices.text: True
False

t_5399602beb88.explanation: Unity calls OnTriggerEnter when the object with the script enters a trigger, provided the trigger interaction requirements are met. Review “Make the pickup a trigger and detect the ball.”

f_b2f946aa0fb7.question: Unity Hub says there is no license, or a project refuses to open. What do I do?
f_b2f946aa0fb7.answer: The license is probably missing or tied to a different Unity ID. First, in Unity Hub click the gear at the top right, choose Licenses, and look for a Unity Personal license. Second, if the list is empty, click Add license, choose the free Unity Personal option and follow the prompts. Third, check that you are signed in with the same Unity ID you used before. Fourth, open the project again from Projects. If it still will not open, ask in the course Q&A forum and say which step you reached.

f_6f4964bdb59f.question: The download or install stops moving, or the Installs list shows it as failed. What do I do?
f_6f4964bdb59f.answer: Large downloads fail when the connection drops or the disk is nearly full. First, check that your internet is working and that you have about 20 GB of free disk space. Second, in Installs, use the retry option on the entry, or click Install Editor again and choose the same version. The install resumes where it stopped. Third, if 6.6 is not listed, use the download archive link on that screen, find 6000.6.4 and click its install button. Fourth, if your computer belongs to a school or employer and blocks the install, ask its IT help desk to install Unity Hub and Unity 6.6. If none of this works, ask in the course Q&A forum.

f_7d967ab62f1d.question: The Editor looks frozen after I click Create project, or my title bar shows another version. What do I do?
f_7d967ab62f1d.answer: If the Editor looks frozen, the first open compiles and imports files and can take five minutes or more. Wait until the progress bar at the bottom of the window is gone. If the title bar does not read like SampleScene - Courtyard - Windows, Mac, Linux - Unity 6.6 (6000.6.4f1), you made the project with the wrong version or template. First, close the Editor. Second, in Unity Hub click New project and check that the Editor version at the top reads 6000.6.4f1 or another 6000.6 version. Third, open the dropdown beside the search box, choose Core and click Universal 3D. Fourth, create the project again as a local project. If creating keeps failing, download the starter project from this page. Ask in the course Q&A forum if that fails too.

f_383feedef9f8.question: My Courtyard looks wrong: an object floats, sinks or lies flat, or the Game view is cropped or cut off. What do I do?
f_383feedef9f8.answer: The cause is almost always one number in the Transform or the camera. First, click the object in the Hierarchy and compare its Position, Rotation and Scale with the list on this page. A new object appears where the Scene view is looking, so every value must be typed. Second, check that Position Y is half the object’s height after scaling. Third, if you cannot see an object in the Scene view, click it in the Hierarchy, move the pointer over the Scene view and press F. Fourth, if the Game view is cut off, click the Game tab and choose 16:9 Aspect. Then select Main Camera and check that Position is 0, 16, -16, Rotation is 45, 0, 0 and Field of View is 60. If it still does not match, open the finished project from this page and compare. Ask in the course Q&A forum and attach a screenshot.

f_78d767e76c96.question: I cannot find Universal 3D in Unity Hub. What do I do?
f_78d767e76c96.answer: You see only the Learning templates. 1. In Unity Hub, click Projects, then New project. 2. Open the dropdown beside the search box. 3. Choose Core. 4. Click Universal 3D. Also check that the Editor version at the top reads 6000.6.4f1, or another 6000.6 version. If it does not, click Installs, then Install Editor, and add Unity 6.6. If the fix does not work, ask in the course Q&A forum.

f_27f5744c8bd3.question: The ball just hangs in the air when I press Play, or it falls straight through the ramp. Why?
f_27f5744c8bd3.answer: If the ball never moves, it has no Rigidbody. 1. Stop Play. 2. Click Ball in the Hierarchy. 3. Click Add Component, type Rigidbody and choose Rigidbody, not Rigidbody 2D. 4. Check that Use Gravity is ticked. If the ball falls through the ramp or floor, a collider is switched off. 1. Stop Play. 2. Tick the checkbox beside Sphere Collider on Ball. 3. Tick the checkbox beside Box Collider on Ramp and Floor. If the ball misses the ramp, check that Ball is at Position 0, 6, -7 and Ramp is at 0, 2, -4. If it still behaves wrongly, ask in the course Q&A forum.

f_8988c99fca08.question: I changed a value while the game was running, and it went back when I stopped. What happened?
f_8988c99fca08.answer: Changes made during Play are thrown away when you stop. This is how Unity works, so nothing is broken. 1. Click Play again to stop the game. The Play button is no longer lit. 2. Select the object in the Hierarchy. 3. Type the value again in the Inspector. 4. Choose File > Save. Make every fix while Play is off. If a value will not stay, ask in the course Q&A forum.

f_4c1722fdb1ad.question: My material color will not change, or the walls are still gray. How do I fix it?
f_4c1722fdb1ad.answer: If the color will not change, you probably clicked a different box. 1. Select the material in the Project window. 2. In the Inspector, find Surface Inputs. 3. Click the color box beside Base Map. 4. In the Color window, click the Hexadecimal box, type the code and press Enter. If the Hexadecimal box is missing, make the window taller and check that the mode dropdown reads RGB 0-255. If an object is still gray, the drag missed it. Drag the material from the Project window onto the object’s name in the Hierarchy, once for each wall. If the color still will not change, ask in the course Q&A forum.

f_904e5faf428b.question: Unity says “All compiler errors have to be fixed before you can enter Play Mode!” and Play will not start. What do I do?
f_904e5faf428b.answer: This means the Console holds at least one red error. Click the Console tab and find the first error in the list. Read its file, line and column, code and sentence, for example Assets/Scripts/Spinner.cs(17,45): error CS1002: ; expected. Double-click the message: Visual Studio Code opens with the cursor on that line. Fix it, and if the line looks fine, check the line above it. Save with Ctrl+S on Windows or Cmd+S on a Mac, click back into Unity and wait for the spinning compile icon to stop. If an old message stays, click Clear. Several errors at once are often one mistake, so fix the first one and look again. If it still fails, compare your file line by line with the code on the page, then ask in the course’s Q&A forum and paste the exact error text.

f_5ba3d23328d2.question: I cannot attach Spinner to the cube. Unity says “No MonoBehaviour scripts in the file, or their names do not match the file name.” What is wrong?
f_5ba3d23328d2.answer: The file name and the class name differ, often by one capital letter. The class inside the file takes the name you typed when you created the script, and Unity matches it to the file name. 1. In the Project window, check the script is called Spinner with a capital S. 2. If it is not, delete the script in the Project window. 3. Choose Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script, type Spinner and press Enter straight away. 4. Wait for Unity to finish compiling, then drag it onto Pickup_Test again, or use Add Component, type Spinner and press Enter. If the problem stays, check the Console for compiler errors, then ask in the course’s Q&A forum.

f_862b5ef3491d.question: I pressed Play and the cube does not move. There is no error. Why?
f_862b5ef3491d.answer: The script runs only when everything is in place. Check these in order. 1. Did you save Spinner.cs? Save with Ctrl+S on Windows or Cmd+S on a Mac, click back into Unity and wait for compiling to finish. 2. Click Pickup_Test and scroll to the bottom of the Inspector. Is there a Spinner (Script) section? If not, attach the script again. 3. Is Is Spinning ticked? 4. Is Speed more than 0? Remember that the Inspector value wins over the number in the code, so a Speed of 0 there will keep the cube still. If you changed a value during Play, it is thrown away when you stop, so change it with Play off. 5. Look in the Scene tab: the Game view may not show the cube. If it still does not move, ask in the course’s Q&A forum and attach a screenshot of the Inspector.

f_3295641a6b79.question: I changed the number in my code, but the cube still turns at the old speed. Which value is used?
f_3295641a6b79.answer: The Inspector value wins. The number in the code is only the starting value, used when the script is first attached. After that the component keeps its own copy. To use the new number from the code, click Pickup_Test, click the three-dot menu in the Spinner (Script) heading and choose Reset. Or type the value you want into Speed in the Inspector. Each cube keeps its own Speed, so check both Pickup_Test and Pickup_Test_B. If the value still looks wrong, ask in the course’s Q&A forum.

f_566de725f3f9.question: I press Play and hold keys, but nothing happens and the Console is empty. What now?
f_566de725f3f9.answer:
You see: the ball sits still and the Console shows no message at all.

1. Click once inside the Game view while Play is on. The Game view must receive your keys.
2. Click Player in the Hierarchy and look for a Player Controller (Script) section in the Inspector. If it is missing, click Add Component, type PlayerController and press Enter.
3. Check that Speed in that section is not 0. The Inspector value wins over the value in the code.
4. Check Update and FixedUpdate for typos in the key names, such as `keyboard.aKey.isPressed`.

If the fix does not work, post in the course Q&A forum with a screenshot of the Inspector and the Console.

f_59dda3abc923.question: The Console shows a red error that says InvalidOperationException about reading Input using the UnityEngine.Input class. What did I do wrong?
f_59dda3abc923.answer:
You see: InvalidOperationException: You are trying to read Input using the UnityEngine.Input class, but you have switched active Input handling to Input System package in Player Settings. The game stops when you press Play.

1. Double-click the red message. The script opens at the line that caused it.
2. Find the line that uses `Input.GetKey` or `Input.GetAxis`. This project uses the Input System package only, so the old Input class cannot be used.
3. Replace it with `Keyboard.current.aKey.isPressed` (with `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;` at the top), or with the Move action: `InputSystem.actions.FindAction("Move")` and `ReadValue<Vector2>()`.
4. Save, wait for the compiling spinner to finish, and press Play again.

If the fix does not work, post your whole script and the error text in the course Q&A forum.

f_1e68175f8025.question: The Console says error CS0246: The type or namespace name ‘Keyboard’ or ‘InputAction’ could not be found. How do I fix it?
f_1e68175f8025.answer:
You see: error CS0246: The type or namespace name ‘Keyboard’ could not be found. The same error can name InputAction instead.

1. Look at the very top of PlayerController.
2. Make sure it contains the line `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;`, spelled exactly like that and ending with a semicolon.
3. Save, and wait for the compiling spinner at the bottom right of the Editor to finish.
4. If the error stays, fix the first error in the Console list. Later errors are often caused by it.

If the fix does not work, post your script and the error in the course Q&A forum.

f_e584780af2c0.question: The ball does not move and the Console shows NullReferenceException. What is empty?
f_e584780af2c0.answer:
You see: NullReferenceException: Object reference not set to an instance of an object. The line it points to is in FixedUpdate, or at the `ReadValue` line.

1. Double-click the error to see which line it points to.
2. If it is in FixedUpdate, `rb` was never filled in. Check that Start contains `rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody>();` and that `private Rigidbody rb;` is declared. Also click Player and check that it has a Rigidbody section (not Rigidbody 2D).
3. If it is at the `ReadValue` line, `FindAction` found nothing. Check that the name in quotes is exactly `"Move"`, with a capital M.
4. Save, wait for the compiling spinner, and press Play again.

If the fix does not work, post your script and a screenshot of the Inspector in the course Q&A forum.

f_3c5eb1d0583f.question: The ball rolls into a pickup and bounces off it. Nothing is counted. What do I do?
f_3c5eb1d0583f.answer:
What you see: the ball is pushed away from the pickup instead of passing through it, and the Console stays empty.
1. Stop Play. Playing with your project changes nothing you set in Play mode, so stop before you edit.
2. In the Hierarchy, click Pickup.
3. In the Inspector, find the Box Collider section and tick Is Trigger.
4. If you made copies of the pickup before ticking it, click each copy and tick Is Trigger there too.
5. Click Play and roll the ball into the pickup again. It should pass through.

f_e42e34c84b05.question: The ball goes through the pickup, but nothing happens. The pickup stays and the Console prints nothing. Why?
f_e42e34c84b05.answer:
What you see: the ball passes through, the pickup stays in the arena, and no message appears.
1. Click the Console tab and check the message icon at the top right is switched on. If it is off, ordinary messages are hidden.
2. Click Player in the Hierarchy. In the Inspector, check that Pickup Collector (Script) is listed. If it is not, click Add Component, type PickupCollector and press Enter.
3. Open PickupCollector and check the method is spelled exactly `void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)`, with a capital T and a capital E. Unity only calls a method with exactly that name.
4. Click the pickup and check its Tag reads Pickup, with a capital P. The word in `other.CompareTag("Pickup")` and the tag must match exactly.
5. If you made copies before you set the tag, click each copy and set its Tag to Pickup. A symptom of this is that only the first pickup works.

f_99201c623559.question: The Console shows a red message that says NullReferenceException when I press Play. What does it mean?
f_99201c623559.answer:
What you see: a red NullReferenceException in the Console, and the score text or the win message does not work.
It means your script is trying to use a text object that is not connected to anything. The field in the Inspector is empty.
1. Click Stop. Do not edit while Play is on, because Unity forgets the change.
2. In the Hierarchy, click Player.
3. In the Inspector, find the Pickup Collector (Script) section.
4. If Score Text is empty, drag ScoreText from the Hierarchy onto it. If Win Text is empty, drag WinText onto it.
5. Choose File > Save, then click Play again.
Read the line in the red message: it names the script and the line number that failed, which tells you which field is empty.

f_7c92d3e6dd7a.question: The Console shows error CS0246 about TMP_Text, or error CS0103 saying a name does not exist. How do I fix a red compile error?
f_7c92d3e6dd7a.answer:
What you see: a red message such as `error CS0246: The type or namespace name 'TMP_Text' could not be found`, or `error CS0103: The name 'scor' does not exist in the current context`. Until the error is fixed, Play will not use your new code.
1. Click the red message in the Console. Visual Studio Code opens at the line with the problem.
2. For CS0246 on TMP_Text, check that the first lines of the file include `using TMPro;`, spelled with those exact capitals.
3. For CS0103, a name is misspelled. Compare it letter by letter with the name where it was first written, near the top of the file. `score` and `scor` are different names.
4. A missing semicolon gives error CS1002: ; expected. Add the semicolon at the end of the line the message points to.
5. Save with Ctrl+S on Windows or Cmd+S on a Mac, return to Unity, and wait for the compiling spinner to stop.
6. If the Console is clean and the game still misbehaves, compare your file with the code on the page, line by line.

# Instructor's version notes: Unity 6.6 (editor 6000.6.4), checked in the editor

Use these names exactly. They are what students see on screen.

## Unity Hub
- Sidebar: Projects, Templates, Installs. Settings is the gear at the top right; licenses are under Settings > Licenses > Add license.
- Projects > New project. The screen opens on the "Learning" templates. Open the dropdown beside the search box and choose "Core" to see Universal 2D, Universal 3D, High Definition 3D and others. The Editor version is chosen at the top of this screen.
- With a template selected, the panel on the right shows: Unity organization, Project name, Location, Use AI Assistant, Use Unity CLI, Source control provider, and the Create project button.
- The Project name box is also a dropdown: "Create new project" (connected to Unity Cloud, the default) or "Create new local project". Students choose "Create new local project", then type the name.
- Clicking Location opens a folder picker with a "Select folder" button.

## A new Universal 3D project
- The window title reads: SampleScene - <project name> - Windows, Mac, Linux - Unity 6.6 (6000.6.4f1).
- Hierarchy: SampleScene with Main Camera, Directional Light and Global Volume.
- Project window, Assets folder: InputSystem_Actions, Readme, Scenes, Settings, TutorialInfo. The scene file is Assets/Scenes/SampleScene.
- On first open the Inspector shows a "URP Empty Template" readme with a "Remove Readme Assets" button.
- Windows in the Default layout: Hierarchy (left), Scene and Game tabs (center), Inspector (right), Project and Console tabs (bottom). Reset with Window > Layouts > Default.

## Menus (top menu bar)
- File: New Scene, Open Scene, Save, Save As..., Build Profiles, Build And Run. There is no "Build Settings" item: the build window is File > Build Profiles.
- Edit: Undo, Redo, Duplicate, Rename, Delete, Play Mode, Project Settings... On a Mac, preferences are Unity > Settings...; on Windows, Edit > Preferences...
- GameObject: Create Empty, Create Empty Child, 2D Object, 3D Object, Visual Effects, Light, Audio, UI Toolkit, UI (Canvas), Camera.
- GameObject > 3D Object: Cube, Sphere, Capsule, Cylinder, Plane, Quad, Text - TextMeshPro.
- GameObject > UI (Canvas): Image, Text - TextMeshPro, Panel, Button - TextMeshPro, Toggle, Slider, Canvas, Event System. The menu is named "UI (Canvas)", not "UI".
- GameObject > Visual Effects: Particle System, Trail, Line. GameObject > Audio: Audio Source. GameObject > Light: Directional Light, Point Light, Spot Light.
- Assets > Create: Folder, Material, MonoBehaviour Script, Scene, Scripting, Physics Material, Input Actions, Animation, 2D, TextMeshPro. A new script is Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script (also under Scripting > MonoBehaviour Script). A scene is Assets > Create > Scene > Scene; a prefab is made by dragging an object from the Hierarchy into the Project window.
- Assets > Create > Animation: Animator Controller, Animation Clip. Window > Animation: Animation, Animator.
- Component > Physics: Rigidbody, Box Collider, Sphere Collider, Capsule Collider, Mesh Collider. Component > Physics 2D: Rigidbody 2D, Box Collider 2D, Circle Collider 2D, Capsule Collider 2D, Composite Collider 2D.
- Window: Layouts, General (Scene, Game, Inspector, Hierarchy, Project, Console), Animation, Audio, Package Management (Package Manager), Rendering, TextMeshPro.

## Code (C#), compiled in this version
- Input: new projects use the Input System package only. `Input.GetAxis`, `Input.GetKey` and the rest of the old Input class compile but throw InvalidOperationException when the game runs. Read keys with `Keyboard.current.aKey.isPressed`, `Keyboard.current.spaceKey.wasPressedThisFrame` (with `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;`), or use the project's own actions: `InputSystem.actions.FindAction("Move")` then `ReadValue<Vector2>()`. The template's InputSystem_Actions asset has a Player map with Move, Look, Attack, Interact, Crouch, Jump, Previous, Next, Sprint.
- Rigidbody: `rb.linearVelocity` and `rb.linearDamping`. `rb.velocity` is marked obsolete.
- Finding objects: `FindAnyObjectByType<T>()`. `FindFirstObjectByType<T>()` and `FindObjectOfType<T>()` are both marked obsolete in 6000.6 and give a yellow warning.
- Text: `using TMPro;` and `TMP_Text`. Scenes: `using UnityEngine.SceneManagement;` and `SceneManager.LoadScene(...)`.
- `AddForce`, `ForceMode.Impulse`, `OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)`, `CompareTag`, `Destroy`, `Instantiate`, `Time.deltaTime`, `[SerializeField]` are unchanged.

## The Inspector, as it reads in this version
- A new object made from the GameObject menu appears where the Scene view is looking, not at the origin: its Position is some uneven number. Students type 0, 0, 0 into Position (or use the three-dot menu on Transform > Reset) before the page gives positions.
- After creating an object or asset its name is in edit mode: type the name and press Enter.
- Every object: name box, Static, Tag, Layer; then Transform with Position, Rotation, Scale (X, Y, Z each).
- A primitive (Cube, Sphere...) has: Transform, a Mesh Filter, Mesh Renderer (Materials, Lighting, Probes, Additional Settings), and its collider (Box Collider, Sphere Collider...). At the bottom is the material, "Lit (Material)", grayed out because the default material cannot be edited, and the Add Component button.
- Sphere Collider: Edit Collider, Is Trigger, Provides Contacts, Material (shows "None (Physics Material)"), Center, Radius, Layer Overrides.
- Add Component opens a small search box: type the name and press Enter. Typing "Rigidbody" lists Rigidbody and Rigidbody 2D.
- Rigidbody: Mass (1), Linear Damping (0), Angular Damping (0.05), Automatic Center Of Mass, Automatic Tensor, Use Gravity (ticked), Is Kinematic, Interpolate (None), Collision Detection (Discrete), Constraints (Freeze Position X Y Z, Freeze Rotation X Y Z), Layer Overrides. There are no fields named "Drag" or "Angular Drag".
- A new material (Assets > Create > Material) uses the shader Universal Render Pipeline/Lit. Its Inspector has Surface Options (Workflow Mode, Surface Type, Render Face, Alpha Clipping, Receive Shadows), Surface Inputs (Base Map with a color box beside it, Metallic Map with a slider, Smoothness with a slider at 0.5, Normal Map, Height Map, Occlusion Map, Emission, Tiling, Offset), Detail Inputs and Advanced Options. The color of a material is the color box beside Base Map; there is no field called "Albedo" or "Color".
- Clicking a color box opens a window titled "Color": a color wheel, a mode dropdown showing "RGB 0-255", sliders R, G, B, A, a box labeled "Hexadecimal", and "Defaults" swatches. The box is "Hexadecimal", not "Hex Color".
- A material is put on an object by dragging it from the Project window onto the object in the Scene view or the Hierarchy.
- Directional Light: Transform (Position 0, 3, 0; Rotation 50, -30, 0), then Light with four sections that open with a triangle: General (Type: Directional, Mode: Realtime), Emission, Rendering, Shadows. Under Emission: Light Appearance (set to "Filter and Temperature"), Filter (a color box), Temperature (a slider, 5000 Kelvin), Intensity (2), Indirect Multiplier, Cookie. To give the light a plain color, set Light Appearance to "Color". There is also a component named Universal Additional Light Data.
- The Scene view has a column of tools at its top left (View, Move, Rotate, Scale, Rect, Transform; keys Q, W, E, R, T, Y) and the scene gizmo at its top right with "Persp" under it. Play, Pause and Step are at the top center of the Editor.
- If a script uses an older API, Unity may show a "Script Updating Consent" dialog offering to update the files: students following the page's code should not see it.
- Edit > Duplicate (Ctrl+D, Command+D on a Mac) names the copy "Ball (1)", selects it and does NOT start a rename. To rename a selected object: Edit > Rename (F2 on Windows, Enter on a Mac), type the name, press Enter.
- A primitive's Inspector reads, in order: Transform, "Cube (Mesh Filter)" (or "Sphere (Mesh Filter)"), Box Collider (or Sphere Collider), Mesh Renderer, then the material.
- A project made from Universal 3D already has these folders in Assets: Materials, Resources, Scenes, Settings, TutorialInfo, and a Readme. Students use the existing Materials folder; they do not create one.
- The Game view's aspect dropdown is the third control in its toolbar and reads "Free Aspect" in a new project. The choice is kept per project: each new project needs "16:9 Aspect" chosen again.
- Changes made during Play to objects in the scene (a Transform, a Rigidbody's Mass) are undone when Play stops. Changes to assets (a material's color or Smoothness, a physics material) are kept.
- An unsaved scene shows an asterisk after its name in the Hierarchy on both systems; do not rely on the window's title bar.
- A new Physics Material (Assets > Create > Physics Material): Dynamic Friction 0.6, Static Friction 0.6, Bounciness 0, Friction Combine Average, Bounce Combine Average. With Bounciness 0.8 and Average against a floor with no material, a ball dropped 6 units bounces once (under 1 unit); with Bounce Combine set to Maximum it bounces eight times or more. A hit slower than 2 units a second does not bounce.
- A new Point Light (GameObject > Light > Point Light): Range 10, Intensity 1, no shadows. At that Intensity it is invisible on a floor 4 units below in a scene lit by the template's sky; Range does not make it brighter. Intensity 30 gives a clear pool of light. Lowering the Directional Light to 0.4 does not make the scene dark, because the sky still lights it.
- A number box takes the keyboard hyphen for a negative value; a typographic minus sign pasted from a page is rejected.
- Opening a project with no internet connection can show a "Packages with Errors" box: Dismiss is safe.
- Timings measured in this version for a 1-unit sphere with a Rigidbody (mass 1) dropped at 0, 6, -7 onto a ramp at 0, 2, -4, rotation 20, 0, 0, scale 6, 0.4, 10 in a 20 by 20 arena with walls 2 high: lands at 0.7 s, leaves the ramp at 2.75 s at 6.5 units a second, reaches the far wall at 4.1 s and rests against it. A mass 10 copy beside it keeps pace exactly.
